cells.tense: Right now, release is what happens after something is actually finished.
cells.act: give it what it needs today, not what it is scheduled for
cells.ask: Take the thing you're done with and set it down today rather than at the date you picked. Let it go while it's still warm.
cells.core:
You can finish a thing and then release it, and that release doesn't cost you much. What you set down when it's complete comes back as room — for the next thing, for rest, for nothing in particular. That's not defeat. It's what finishing looks like on the way out.

Where you decide what stays and what goes, your timing is sound: the grip loosens when the work is done, not before, and not after out of habit. Sometimes there's a young thing inside what you're finishing — a version still taking shape — and it doesn't need a verdict yet. It needs to not be judged while it's small. Give it what it actually needs today, not what you scheduled. The rest goes when it goes.
cells.sheetLine: You finish it, then you let it go.
cells.place: where you choose what to keep and what to set down

cells.tense: You will be handing things away before they are finished, and you will call it grace.
cells.act: do the plain version first, before the plans
cells.ask: Before you release the next thing, do the plain version of it once — no plan, no refinement. See what's actually there.
cells.core:
Somewhere in you, release has gotten ahead of finishing. You'll be handing something off — a role, a person, an outcome — and calling it surrender, and the finish hasn't happened yet. There's a version of this where the release is clean, but this version is quicker than that. It reads as grace from outside and feels like a countdown from inside.

Where you decide what stays and what goes, steady practice is what steadies it. Stay in the plain work one more round before you decide anything. That's not clinging. It's the opposite of a dramatic letting go: you do the ordinary thing again, alone, until it tells you what it is. Then the release is fine. The hurry is the part that isn't.
cells.sheetLine: You're releasing things before they've finished happening.
cells.place: where you choose what to keep and what to set down

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you a while back.
cells.act: carry it without tightening around it
cells.ask: Take the load you're gripping hardest and carry it today without adding tension. Same weight, looser arms.
cells.core:
Where you decide what stays and what goes, the deciding has gone quiet. Things stay held long after the reason for holding them stopped being true, and the strain itself is what's tiring — not the things. You can still set something down; the muscle for it has just gone unused. That's not a character flaw. It's a door that stopped being opened.

What helps isn't a big release. Carry one load you've got in hand without tightening around it. Same weight, looser arms. You don't have to decide anything about it yet, and you don't have to do it well. Hold your shape — that's the whole move. The grip eases once it stops being the thing you're managing.
cells.sheetLine: You've been holding things you stopped choosing.
cells.place: where you choose what to keep and what to set down

cells.tense: You have already let go of some things and still believe you are the one holding on.
cells.act: make room for it without steering it
cells.ask: Take stock of what's actually in your hands — one load you're carrying, one you're not. Just the difference, no decision.
cells.core:
You've told yourself a story about what you're still holding, and some of it isn't true anymore. There are things you released months ago and still think you're carrying — and things you think you've set down that are still in your hands. The deciding keeps happening underneath the account you give of it.

Make room for the actual thing, without steering it toward either answer. You don't need to decide which category anything belongs in. Just look at what's in your hands today and notice which is which. Care for it the way you'd care for anything still small — ask nothing of it, judge it early and it'll hide. The point isn't to file things away. It's catching yourself mid-sort.
cells.sheetLine: You've let go of more than you think you have.
cells.place: where you choose what to keep and what to set down
